label: Barbara H. Rosenwein
description: A medieval historian whose studies of property, immunity and power led to an influential approach to the history of emotions. ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) revisits Lucien Febvre’s call for a history of feeling and rejects the grand narrative, associated with Norbert Elias, of a movement from unrestrained medieval emotion to modern self-control. In its place she proposes emotional communities: overlapping groups that value and express emotions in different ways. In a 2010 interview she questions William Reddy’s sharp distinction between emotional regimes and emotional refuges; Reddy’s reply allowing plural regimes stands beside her objection. Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) is the book-length study.

label: J. R. Miller
description: A settler historian of Indigenous–newcomer relations, residential schooling and treaties in Canada. Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) is his history of Indian–white relations in Canada. label: Patrick J. Geary
description: A medieval historian of relics, memory and ethnic identity. Furta Sacra (1978) studied thefts of relics in the central Middle Ages, and his essay ‘Sacred Commodities’ (1986) asks what made relics exchangeable within a particular medieval setting rather than assuming a timeless market. Phantoms of Remembrance (1994) concerns memory and oblivion at the end of the first millennium. The Myth of Nations (2002) uses research on changing early medieval identities to criticize modern nationalist claims to ancient continuity; Steven Fanning credits its central argument while warning that its survey contains questionable assertions and broad generalizations.

label: Robert Bartlett
description: A medieval historian of conquest, law and historical categories. Trial by Fire and Water (1986) studied the medieval judicial ordeal, and The Making of Europe (1993) traced conquest, colonization and cultural change between 950 and 1350. His 2001 article on race and ethnicity treats both terms as social constructions and warns against using present administrative labels as ready-made historical explanations. Comparing medieval terminology, he emphasizes culture, law, language and religion in the making of identities, while examining genealogical idioms of descent, and separates collective identity from any automatic demand for sovereign statehood. Geraldine Heng later questions the sharpness of his distinction between medieval cultural difference and biological racism.

label: Bruce G. Trigger
description: A Canadian archaeologist and ethnohistorian of the Wendat (Huron) and of colonial encounters in northeastern North America. The Children of Aataentsic (1976) combines archaeology, history and ethnology to argue that Iroquoian societies had changed substantially in the centuries before European contact, so that the impact of contact cannot be assessed without understanding that earlier change. Natives and Newcomers (1985) reconsiders Canada’s ‘heroic age’ of exploration and colonization in the same way, and A History of Archaeological Thought (1989) is his history of his own discipline. He wrote the foreword to Georges E. Sioui’s For an Amerindian Autohistory (1992). Emma LaRocque criticizes that foreword as an example of containment, and argues that the cross-cultural approach to which Trigger belonged, though an improvement on earlier racist scholarship, could still distance and Other its subjects.

label: Callum G. Brown
description: A social and cultural historian of religion, secularisation and unbelief. Brown’s work moved from class-based measurements of church participation toward the gendered and discursive conditions of Christian identity, with a sharp rupture proposed for the 1960s. That account remains contested. Jeremy Morris accepts criticism of inevitable modernization-to-decline stories while arguing that Brown and others narrow religion too far: institutional decline can coexist with persistent religious identity. Brown’s later “The Necessity of Atheism” approaches the problem from another direction. Using Charles Taylor as a critical foil, he argues that measuring secularity only through religious categories marginalizes lives lived without a god and that medieval disbelief should not be ruled out in advance. The intervention challenges both the assumed religious past and the categories used to describe the secular present; it does not establish a single universal measure of unbelief.

description: A historian of medicine and science. The Cholera Years (1962), on the United States in 1832, 1849 and 1866, is credited with leading historians to study not only a disease and its victims but society’s response to it, through politics, law and social mores. edges.relationship: In ‘Disease in History: Frames and Framers’ (1989) Rosenberg calls the social construction of illness ‘in an important sense … no more than a tautology’, avoids the term because it overemphasizes functionalist ends and arbitrariness, and argues that the main trends in the history of disease, social-control readings among them, lose sight of the process of disease definition itself and its consequences.
edges.evidence_note: His own text, read in the Milbank Memorial Fund's open archive copy of The Milbank Quarterly 67, Suppl. 1 (1989), pp. 1–15. p. 2: ‘Much has been written during the past two decades about the social construction of illness. But in an important sense this is no more than a tautology’; the position ‘still serves to remind us’ that medical thought is rarely free of social constraint. p. 3: ‘I have, in fact, avoided the term social construction. I felt it has tended to overemphasize functionalist ends and the degree of arbitrariness’ and focused on ‘a handful of socially resonant diagnoses’; he uses ‘the less programmatically charged metaphor “frame”’. pp. 3–4 list five trends in disease history (social history; public health and the demographic transition; an ecological ‘new materialism’; demography; and, ‘perhaps most widely influential’, disease definitions as ‘a tool of social control’, citing Wright and Treacher 1982 and Figlio 1978, in which physicians are construed as agents of ‘a broader hegemonic enterprise’); p. 4: ‘What is often lost sight of in each of these emphases—and in the aggregate in all—is the process of disease definition itself’ and its consequences. The ‘lost sight of’ sentence applies to all five trends, not to social-control readings alone. A critique within a field he also built (his contribution edge edge_2946 remains): it qualifies the constructionist and social-control strands of medical history, it does not reject social history of medicine, which he calls necessarily ‘social’ (p. 3). The essay was reprinted as the introduction to Framing Disease (with Janet Golden, 1992) and in Explaining Epidemics (1992); those reprints were not collated. Named targets (Wright, Treacher, Figlio) are not atlas endpoints.

label: J. R. McNeill
description: An environmental historian who works at global and regional scales. Something New Under the Sun (2000) is an environmental history of the twentieth-century world. Mosquito Empires (2010) argues that ecological change made the Greater Caribbean hospitable to the mosquitoes that carry yellow fever and malaria. Because survivors gained immunity or resistance, these diseases took sides in the struggles for empire and revolution between 1620 and 1914, decimating forces sent from Europe. His survey of the field credits the Annales with an inspiring general approach while noting how little environmental history its founders wrote, and treats Alfred Crosby’s studies of ecological exchange as landmarks. In his 2020 AHA presidential address he argues that scientific evidence can illuminate histories poorly documented in writing, while warning against monocausal climate histories and against letting a new tool dictate the question.

label: Joanna Bourke
description: A historian of modern Britain, war, the body and emotion. Dismembering the Male (1996) studies men’s bodies and masculinity in the First World War. An Intimate History of Killing (1999), drawing on letters, diaries and memoirs of British, American and Australian combatants in the two world wars and Vietnam, argues that the structure of war encouraged pleasure in killing and that ordinary men could become enthusiastic killers without being brutalized. Her later work on fear and pain asks what emotions do: expressions of fear follow learned conventions yet can change the feeling they name, a point she develops through William Reddy’s concept of the emotive.

label: John M. MacKenzie
description: A historian of empire who made its cultural presence in Britain, and its environmental history overseas, central subjects of imperial history. As founding editor of Manchester University Press’s Studies in Imperialism series he set out to examine how imperialism shaped the dominant societies as well as those they ruled; Propaganda and Empire (1984) studied the manipulation of British public opinion. The Empire of Nature (1988) connected hunting and conservation with British rule in Africa and India. Orientalism: History, Theory and the Arts (1995) challenged Edward Said’s generalizations through empirical study of the arts, as Berny Sèbe describes; Said in turn criticized an approach he associated with MacKenzie that treated culture as propaganda. His exchanges with Bernard Porter, after Porter’s The Absent-Minded Imperialists (2004), became among the most-read items in the Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History.

label: Paul Kennedy
description: A historian of international power, strategy and political economy. The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987) argues that great powers decline relative to others when their strategic commitments outrun their economic base; readers summarized this as ‘imperial overstretch’, and in the late 1980s it was read as a warning to the United States. Michael Cox notes that the idea was not wholly new, and Kennedy himself traced one stimulus to Mahan’s use of an earlier reflection on Spain’s dispersed empire. In the same roundtable Varsha Venkatasubramanian criticized the book’s neglect of non-state actors and of politics’ effects on economic development; Kennedy accepted her point about India and conceded that the book may contain too much economic determinism. His earlier books studied British naval mastery and the Anglo-German antagonism before 1914.

label: Paul Thompson
description: A social and oral historian concerned with how interviews change both historical evidence and research practice. His retrospective interview credits Townsend’s socially engaged research and George Ewart Evans’s listening methods, and recalls resisting Hobsbawm’s request to remove oral-history material from The Edwardians. Thompson distinguishes his early emphasis on reliable recollection from later attention to subjectivity, silence and memory associated with Passerini and Portelli. His community-history discussion also warns that participation can exclude less confident people and need not produce progressive politics. Becky Taylor’s reassessment credits the fishing project’s attention to change and its preservation of sources, while questioning interview schedules, uneven transcription and the insufficiently examined category of fisherman. Her reuse demonstrates how an archive can support questions its makers did not fully pursue. Living the Fishing was collaborative work with Tony Wailey and Trevor Lummis, not Thompson’s solitary project.

label: Stephen Greenblatt
description: A literary scholar and theorist whose New Historicism reads literature within the whole field of a period’s culture. Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980) examines how More, Tyndale, Wyatt, Spenser, Marlowe and Shakespeare fashioned selves, finding that new questions about identity shaped sixteenth-century writing. He calls New Historicism ‘madly eclectic’: it grew from impatience with American formalism and with Marxist criticism, and drew on Foucault to escape the base/superstructure dichotomy, as well as on Walter Benjamin, Michel de Certeau and Clifford Geertz. He credits Raymond Williams with showing how to connect art to the world in which it is made. Sarah Maza questions how far New Historicism and historians’ cultural history actually meet across disciplinary lines, and John Monfasani criticized The Swerve for opposing medieval darkness to Renaissance modernity; Greenblatt replied defending the Renaissance and the importance of atomism.

label: T. M. Devine

label: Thomas W. Laqueur
description: A cultural historian of the body, sexuality and death. Making Sex (1990) argues that a ‘one-sex’ model, in which men and women were thought to share the same basic body, gave way in the eighteenth century to a ‘two-sex’ model grounded in biological difference: sex difference itself has a history. The thesis has been both influential and contested. Brooke Holmes, drawing on work by Katharine Park, Robert Nye, Joan Cadden and Helen King, argues that the evidence shows more varied and coexisting models, and traces the book’s narrative of epochal rupture to Foucault’s history of sexuality. Caroline Walker Bynum drew on it while noting Park and Nye’s qualification. Solitary Sex (2003) is a cultural history of masturbation, and The Work of the Dead (2015) asks what the care and naming of the dead do for the living.
